questions.stem: Personality is best described as:
options: a person's characteristic patterns of thinking, feeling and behaving
a person's level of intelligence measured on a standardised test
a person's temporary mood in response to a particular situation
a person's physical health and their level of fitness over time
questions.explanation: Personality refers to the relatively consistent network of emotions, cognitive processes and behaviours that make each person distinct. A passing mood is a temporary state rather than personality.

questions.stem: Why is personality described as a socially and culturally constructed concept?
options: Which traits are noticed and valued differs between societies and cultures
Personality is fixed at birth and is expressed the same way in every culture
Personality can be measured directly by a blood test or brain scan
Only Western cultures have people with distinct personalities
questions.explanation: What counts as a desirable or meaningful trait, and even the idea of a stable individual personality, varies between cultures. For example, assertiveness may be admired in one culture and seen as rude in another.

questions.stem: In Freud's psychodynamic approach, which part of personality operates on the pleasure principle and seeks immediate gratification?
options: the ideal self
the id
the ego
the superego
questions.explanation: The id is the unconscious, instinctive part of personality that demands immediate satisfaction. The ego works on the reality principle and the superego represents moral standards.

questions.stem: A hungry student wants to grab a friend's lunch, feels it would be wrong, and instead buys food at the canteen. In Freud's terms, which part of personality found this compromise?
options: the ego
the id
the superego
the unconscious
questions.explanation: The ego mediates between the id's demands and the superego's moral standards, finding a realistic way to satisfy needs. The id wanted the lunch and the superego objected; the ego found a workable solution.

questions.stem: A central idea of the psychodynamic approach is that:
options: unconscious conflicts, often from childhood, shape adult personality
people are naturally motivated to grow and fulfil their potential
personality can be described by scores on a few broad dimensions
behaviour is fully explained by rewards and punishments in the present
questions.explanation: Freud proposed that much of personality is driven by unconscious desires and conflicts, many rooted in early childhood. Striving to fulfil potential is the humanistic view, and broad dimensions are the trait view.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest scientific criticism of Freud's psychodynamic approach?
options: It was based on large, random samples from many different cultures
Its key ideas are hard to test because unconscious processes cannot be observed
It was the first approach to suggest that childhood experiences matter
It focuses only on conscious choices and ignores unconscious motives
questions.explanation: Concepts such as the id and repression are difficult to measure or falsify, and Freud's theory was based largely on case studies of a small number of patients. Recognising the influence of childhood is usually counted as a strength.

questions.stem: In Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which need sits at the top?
options: love and belonging
safety
self-actualisation
esteem
questions.explanation: Maslow placed self-actualisation, realising one's full potential, at the top. Physiological, safety, love and belonging, and esteem needs come before it.

questions.stem: According to Maslow, why might a student who is often hungry and unsafe at home struggle to focus on achieving at school?
options: School achievement is a physiological need at the base of the hierarchy
Unconscious conflicts from childhood prevent any form of achievement
Lower needs must be largely met before higher needs motivate behaviour
Higher needs must be met before lower needs can be felt at all
questions.explanation: Maslow proposed that basic physiological and safety needs dominate until they are reasonably satisfied. Only then do esteem needs, such as achievement, become strong motivators.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the humanistic approach to personality?
options: Personality is determined by unconscious drives formed in early childhood
Personality is best described by measuring stable, inherited traits
Personality is shaped mainly by conditioning from the environment
People have free will and a natural drive towards personal growth
questions.explanation: Humanistic psychologists such as Maslow and Rogers emphasise free will, the individual's subjective experience and the drive to fulfil potential. They reacted against the more pessimistic psychodynamic view.

questions.stem: Which is a weakness of Maslow's humanistic approach?
options: Self-actualisation is vaguely defined and was based on a small, selected group
It gives too much weight to unconscious sexual and aggressive drives
It reduces personality to a small number of measurable dimensions
It treats people as passive and unable to make their own choices
questions.explanation: Maslow described self-actualisation by studying people he admired, which makes the concept subjective and hard to test. The hierarchy may also not apply across cultures that value the group over the individual.

questions.stem: The trait approach to personality aims to:
options: explain personality as a set of conditioned responses to stimuli
describe personality using stable characteristics that can be measured
explain personality through unconscious conflicts and defence mechanisms
understand personality through a person's drive to self-actualise
questions.explanation: Trait theorists identify relatively stable dimensions, such as extraversion, and measure how much of each a person has. Unconscious conflicts belong to the psychodynamic approach.

questions.stem: Which list gives the five factors in the Big Five, or five-factor, model?
options: optimism, conscientiousness, empathy, agreeableness, neuroticism
openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, assertiveness, intelligence
openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism
openness, confidence, extraversion, ambition, nervousness
questions.explanation: The Big Five factors are openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism, often remembered as OCEAN.

questions.stem: Eysenck's trait theory described personality in terms of broad dimensions. Which two did he propose first?
options: openness to experience and conscientiousness
honesty-humility and emotionality
the ideal self and the real self
extraversion-introversion and neuroticism-stability
questions.explanation: Eysenck began with two dimensions, extraversion-introversion and neuroticism-emotional stability, and later added psychoticism. Openness and conscientiousness are from the Big Five; honesty-humility is from HEXACO.

questions.stem: How does the HEXACO model differ from the five-factor model?
options: It adds honesty-humility, giving six broad dimensions
It removes extraversion and replaces it with intelligence
It describes personality in terms of the id, ego and superego
It is a projective test using ambiguous pictures and inkblots
questions.explanation: HEXACO stands for honesty-humility, emotionality, extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness to experience. Its honesty-humility factor emerged from lexical studies in several languages, which is one reason it is used in cross-cultural research.

questions.stem: A critic says the trait approach describes personality well but does not explain it. What is the critic's main point?
options: Traits cannot be measured, so the approach has no scientific support
Traits are based entirely on unconscious processes that cannot be observed
Trait scores show what a person is like but not why they developed that way
Trait scores are unreliable because they change completely from week to week
questions.explanation: Trait theories are good at measuring and comparing people and predicting some behaviour, but say little about how traits develop. They are also criticised for underestimating how situations shape behaviour.

questions.stem: Why has the five-factor model been considered deficient in some cross-cultural research?
options: Its factors came mainly from Western, English-language studies and may miss traits valued elsewhere
Its factors are identical in every culture, so there is nothing left to compare
It can only be used with clinical patients who have a personality disorder
It relies on inkblot responses that cannot be translated into other languages
questions.explanation: The model was developed largely from Western samples, and some cultures show traits, such as interpersonal relatedness, that the five factors do not capture well. The factors replicate in many cultures, but not perfectly.

questions.stem: Which personality assessment asks people to answer standard questions about themselves, with responses compared to norms?
options: a projective inkblot test
a standardised self-report inventory
a behavioural observation
a clinical interview
questions.explanation: Self-report inventories such as the MMPI-2 or the NEO-PI-R present the same items to everyone and compare scores with those of a norm group.

questions.stem: What is a main disadvantage of standardised self-report inventories?
options: They take far longer to score than a clinical interview
They cannot be compared with scores from other people
They can only be used by observing people in public
People may answer in ways that make them look good
questions.explanation: Self-reports rely on honest and accurate self-knowledge, so answers can be distorted by social desirability or limited insight. They are quick to score and compare, which is a strength.

questions.stem: A psychologist records how often a child shares toys during free play over several days. What is an advantage of this behavioural observation?
options: It is quick and costs very little compared with a questionnaire
It removes any chance of the observer affecting the behaviour
It records what the child actually does rather than what they say
It reveals the child's unconscious motives behind their behaviour
questions.explanation: Observation provides direct evidence of behaviour, which is especially useful with young children. However, it is time-consuming, and being watched may change behaviour.

questions.stem: What is a main advantage of a clinical interview as a personality assessment?
options: Every person is asked exactly the same questions, so scores are comparable
It provides data that are entirely objective and quantitative
The interviewer can follow up answers and explore issues in depth
The interviewer's own views can never affect the conclusions drawn
questions.explanation: Clinical interviews are flexible and give rich information, but because they are less structured, they rely on the interviewer's judgement and can be biased.

questions.stem: A personality test gives a person very similar scores when taken two weeks apart, but scores do not relate to how the person actually behaves. The test is:
options: reliable but not valid
valid but not reliable
both reliable and valid
neither reliable nor valid
questions.explanation: Reliability is consistency of results, which this test shows. Validity is whether it measures what it claims to, and failing to relate to actual behaviour suggests it does not.

questions.stem: An online quiz claims to reveal personality from which of four pictures a person prefers. Why is it likely to have lower validity than a standardised self-report inventory?
options: It is scored by a computer, so results cannot be checked for errors
It has not been tested against established measures or actual behaviour
It asks people about their own behaviour, so it is open to social desirability
It has been given to a large norm group, so individual scores are diluted
questions.explanation: Standardised inventories are developed and checked to show they measure what they claim and compare with norms. An untested picture quiz has no such evidence.

questions.stem: Which is an ethical issue that must be considered when giving someone a personality assessment?
options: The results must be shared with the person's employer and family
The person must complete the test even if they wish to stop
The results must be kept confidential and used only for the agreed purpose
The person must not be told what the assessment results will be used for
questions.explanation: Ethical assessment requires informed consent, confidentiality, use of the data only for the stated purpose, and the right to withdraw. Results should be explained by a qualified person.

questions.stem: Which pairing of approach and preferred assessment is most accurate?
options: humanistic theorists: behavioural counts in laboratory experiments
trait theorists: standardised self-report inventories of stable traits
trait theorists: unstructured interviews exploring unconscious conflicts
psychodynamic theorists: self-report inventories scored against norms
questions.explanation: Trait theorists favour inventories that measure stable traits on scales. Psychodynamic theorists prefer methods aimed at the unconscious, such as projective tests and clinical interviews, and humanistic theorists value the person's own view of themselves.

questions.stem: Assertiveness is best described as:
options: expressing your needs and views honestly while respecting others
getting your own way by intimidating or blaming other people
avoiding conflict by always going along with other people's wishes
keeping your feelings hidden so that nobody is ever upset
questions.explanation: Assertive communication is direct and honest but respectful. Intimidating others is aggressive, and always giving in is passive.

questions.stem: In assertiveness training, a person practises saying 'I feel frustrated when meetings run late because I miss my bus' rather than 'You always waste my time'. Why?
options: I-statements avoid mentioning the speaker's feelings altogether
I-statements let the speaker blame others more clearly
I-statements express feelings without attacking the other person
I-statements make the speaker appear more aggressive and powerful
questions.explanation: I-statements describe one's own feelings and the specific behaviour, which is less likely to make the listener defensive than an accusing you-statement. This helps resolve problems and improves relationships.

questions.stem: How could assertiveness training promote personal growth?
options: By replacing all communication with written instructions
By building confidence to express needs and set boundaries
By teaching people to suppress their views to avoid conflict
By encouraging people to dominate others in group settings
questions.explanation: Learning to state needs and say no respectfully can raise self-esteem, reduce stress and improve relationships. Suppressing views is passive communication, which assertiveness training aims to change.

questions.stem: How can understanding the similarities and differences between people promote personal growth?
options: It can increase self-awareness and acceptance of others' styles
It shows that personality is fixed, so change is not possible
It proves that one personality type is better than all others
It removes the need to adapt to other people at work or school
questions.explanation: Knowing one's own traits and recognising that others differ can help a person build on strengths, manage weaknesses and work better with people unlike themselves.

questions.stem: Personality disorders can be described as:
options: the normal changes in personality that occur during adolescence
personality differences that exist only between cultures
exaggerations of personality traits to inflexible, dysfunctional levels
short episodes of low mood that pass within a few days without treatment
questions.explanation: A personality disorder involves an enduring, inflexible pattern of thinking, feeling and behaving that differs markedly from cultural expectations and causes distress or impairment.

questions.stem: Which explanation of borderline personality disorder uses a biopsychosocial model?
options: Inherited emotional sensitivity, poor emotion regulation and an invalidating upbringing
A single inherited gene that causes the disorder whatever a person experiences
Poor choices made by the person, which they could stop at any time if they wanted
A lack of willpower that develops in adolescence from too much screen time
questions.explanation: The biopsychosocial model combines biological factors such as temperament, psychological factors such as emotion regulation, and social factors such as early trauma or an invalidating environment.

questions.stem: Stigma towards people with personality disorders refers to:
options: the formal process that clinicians use to diagnose the disorder
the positive traits that help a person cope with their disorder
a treatment that reduces symptoms by changing unhelpful thoughts
negative stereotypes and devaluing of people because of their diagnosis
questions.explanation: Stigma involves labelling and negative beliefs, such as that people with a diagnosis are manipulative or dangerous, which can lead to discrimination and reluctance to seek help.

questions.stem: Films often portray people with a personality disorder as dangerous or manipulative. Which is the most likely effect of this on the individual?
options: They may feel ashamed and avoid seeking help
They will become more willing to talk openly
They will be offered more support by others
They will receive faster and more accurate diagnosis
questions.explanation: Media stereotypes contribute to public stigma, which people can internalise as shame and low self-worth. This makes them less likely to disclose their condition or seek treatment.

questions.stem: Which strategy is most likely to reduce the stigma associated with personality disorders?
options: showing only the most extreme cases so the public takes them seriously
contact with people with lived experience and accurate media portrayals
describing people only by their diagnosis to make it easy to identify
avoiding all public discussion of mental illness to protect privacy
questions.explanation: Education, respectful person-first language, contact with people who have lived experience and accurate media portrayals all challenge stereotypes. Silence and extreme portrayals reinforce them.

questions.stem: A researcher randomly assigns participants to post either anonymously or under their real name in an online forum, then counts hostile comments. Which statement is correct?
options: It is a qualitative design because it uses a focus group to discuss hostility
It is a correlational design because personality traits are measured as variables
It is an experiment because anonymity is manipulated as the independent variable
It is an observational design because comments are counted in a natural setting
questions.explanation: The researcher deliberately changes whether posts are anonymous and measures the effect on hostile comments, so it is experimental. Such a study could test the online disinhibition effect.

questions.stem: Which is an observational design for studying personality?
options: giving half the group a drug and half a placebo, then comparing
manipulating noise levels to see how introverts perform on a test
recording and rating children's sociability during lunch breaks
assigning participants to two conditions and changing a variable
questions.explanation: Observational designs describe or measure behaviour as it occurs without manipulating variables. The other options all involve a manipulated independent variable.

questions.stem: Why might research on personality raise ethical concerns about privacy?
options: Personality data can only be collected using deception
Personality data can reveal sensitive information about a person
Personality data cannot be stored for any length of time
Personality data are always collected without the person's knowledge
questions.explanation: Personality results may reveal private characteristics or mental health concerns, so they must be kept confidential and used only for the purpose consented to.
